en.title: Rights and duties
en.summary: Laws, rights and responsibilities of citizens, and the modal verbs of obligation.

paragraphs: Rights and duties are two sides of citizenship. This lesson uses the modal verbs of obligation and permission, which are the language of laws and rules.
A teacher is explaining citizenship to a class in Belfast.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Everyone has the right to education and to a fair trial.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: We must obey the law and respect the rights of other people.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: No, you don't have to, but you should. In some countries voting is compulsory, but not here.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: You can vote in elections when you are eighteen, and you must be registered first.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Most adults can be asked to do jury service, and they must attend unless they have a good reason.

paragraphs: **1. Must, have to, don't have to and mustn't differ in meaning.** Must and have to express obligation; don't have to means it is not necessary; mustn't means it is forbidden. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
FormMeaningExample
must / have toobligationWe must obey the law.
don't have tonot necessaryYou don't have to vote.
mustn'tforbiddenYou mustn't steal.
can / maypermissionYou can vote at eighteen.

paragraphs: **2. The right to + noun or verb.** The phrase takes a noun or an infinitive. See Introduction to Grammar: Verbs and verb phrases.

blocks.html:
PatternExample
the right to + nounthe right to education
the right to + verbthe right to vote
a duty to + verba duty to pay tax
the responsibility forthe responsibility for your actions

items: A citizen belongs to a country; a resident lives in it.
Jury service is a duty in some countries to help decide a court case.
Vote means to choose in an election; a register of voters lists those who can vote.

paragraphs: In the United Kingdom the voting age is eighteen and voting is not compulsory; in Australia it is. Citizens also have the right to protest peacefully, provided that they follow the law.
